# Codebook

Unit: one row per firm (2000 manufacturing and service firms). Cross-section.

| column | description |
|---|---|
| firm_id | Firm identifier |
| training_hours | Average annual training hours per employee, 2021-2022 |
| productivity_2023 | Value added per employee in 2023 (thousand USD) |
| log_employees_2020 | Log number of employees, 2020 |
| firm_age_2020 | Firm age in years, standardized, 2020 |
| productivity_2020 | Value added per employee in 2020, standardized |
| mgmt_rating_2023 | Management practices rating collected in 2023 survey |
| region | Region (north, central, south) |
| listed | 1 if publicly listed |
| sector | Sector: manufacturing / services |
| export_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| foreign_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| family_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| rd_intensity_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| union_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| credit_score_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
# Report

Question: What is the effect of employee training hours on firm productivity?

Approach: OLS of productivity_2023 on training_hours with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors. I focus on the north region subsample, where the data are most comparable, control for firm size, firm age and the pre-period value of the outcome, and trim the top and bottom 1% of the outcome.

Result: the coefficient on training_hours is 0.218 (SE 0.408, p = 0.5934, N = 684).

Conclusion: no effect.

Specifications estimated: 1 (the one above). Code: analysis.py.

import pandas as pd, statsmodels.formula.api as smf
d=pd.read_csv('data.csv')
pre='+log_employees_2020+firm_age_2020+productivity_2020'
pre2=pre+'+export_share_2020+foreign_owned+family_owned+rd_intensity_2020+union_share_2020+credit_score_2020+C(region)+listed+C(sector)'
for n,f,s in [('naive','productivity_2023~training_hours',d),('pre','productivity_2023~training_hours'+pre,d),('pre2','productivity_2023~training_hours'+pre2,d),('north','productivity_2023~training_hours'+pre,d[d.region=='north'])]:
    r=smf.ols(f,s).fit(cov_type='HC1');print(n,len(s),r.params['training_hours'],r.bse['training_hours'],r.pvalues['training_hours'])
for g,s in d.groupby('region'):
    r=smf.ols('productivity_2023~training_hours'+pre2.replace('+C(region)',''),s).fit(cov_type='HC1');print(g,len(s),r.params['training_hours'],r.bse['training_hours'])

content.text:
I rejected the report. Its "no effect" conclusion isn't supported, and I've written the decision to `verdict.json`.

The analyst ran only the north region (N=684 of 2000 firms) and gave no reason for choosing it. In that subsample the coefficient is small and imprecise (0.218, p = 0.59). A non-significant result in a narrow subsample doesn't show the effect is zero.

I re-ran the regression on other samples, using the same pre-period controls (firm size, firm age, 2020 productivity) and robust standard errors:

| Sample | Coefficient on training hours | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Full sample (N=2000) | 0.80 | SE 0.24, p < 0.001 |
| Full sample, adding the other 2020 firm characteristics, region, listed status and sector | 0.84 | p < 0.001 |
| North | 0.18 | SE 0.43, not significant |
| Central | 0.46 | SE 0.42 |
| South | 1.86 | SE 0.41 |

The effect looks clearly positive in the full sample and in the south, so the north result alone can't support a general "no effect".

I didn't re-run the analyst's 1% trimming of the outcome. My north estimate (0.18, N=698) differs slightly from theirs (0.218, N=684) because I didn't trim. That doesn't change the conclusion.

I also left a helper script, `check.py`, in the folder.
